topics.title: The cell cycle and its two phases

learn.hook: A human cell in culture takes about 24 hours to divide, but spends only about one hour actually dividing. What is it doing the other 23?
points: The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and finally divides into two daughter cells. Cell growth is continuous, but DNA synthesis occurs in only one specific stage.
Human cells in culture divide about once every 24 hours; yeast can complete a cycle in only about 90 minutes. Duration varies between organisms and cell types.
Two basic phases: interphase (between two M phases) and M phase (mitosis phase, when actual division occurs). In a 24-hour human cycle, M phase lasts only about an hour.
M phase starts with nuclear division (karyokinesis, separation of daughter chromosomes) and usually ends with division of cytoplasm (cytokinesis).
Interphase, often called the resting phase, takes more than 95% of the cycle. It is not idle: the cell grows and replicates DNA in an orderly way. It has three sub-phases: G1, S and G2.

example.q: In a 24-hour human cell cycle with M phase lasting 1 hour, what percentage of the cycle is interphase?
steps: Interphase = 24 - 1 = 23 hours.

learn.reallife: Cancer drugs used at the Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai often target dividing cells in specific phases of the cell cycle.

topics.title: G1, S, G2 and G0: inside interphase

learn.hook: Heart muscle cells mostly stop dividing in adults. They park in a special 'waiting room' of the cell cycle called G0.
points: G1 (Gap 1): between mitosis and the start of DNA replication. The cell is metabolically active and grows but does not replicate its DNA.

S phase (synthesis): DNA replicates and the DNA content doubles from 2C to 4C, but the chromosome number stays the same (2n stays 2n). In animal cells, DNA replication begins in the nucleus and the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.
G2 (Gap 2): proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis, and cell growth continues.
Quiescent stage (G0): cells that stop dividing (e.g. heart cells) exit G1 into G0. They remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless needed.
In animals, mitosis occurs only in diploid somatic cells. Plants can show mitosis in both haploid and diploid cells.

example.q: A diploid cell has 2n = 8 and DNA content 2C in G1. Give the chromosome number and DNA content after S phase.
steps: S phase doubles DNA: 2C → 4C.
Each chromosome now has two chromatids, but the number of chromosomes is unchanged: 2n = 8.

learn.reallife: Liver cells usually sit in G0 but can re-enter the cycle after injury, which is why living-donor liver transplants at Indian hospitals work: the donated part regrows.

learn.hook: Cytogenetics labs make karyotypes from cells stopped at metaphase, because chromosomes are then at their most compact and clearest.
points: M phase is also called equational division because parent and daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes. Mitosis is described in four stages of karyokinesis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase), though it is a continuous process.

Prophase: chromatin condenses into compact mitotic chromosomes, each with two chromatids joined at the centromere. The centrosome (duplicated in S phase) moves to opposite poles; each radiates microtubules called asters; asters and spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus.
At the end of prophase, the Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope are no longer visible.

Metaphase begins with complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope. Chromosomes are fully condensed, so morphology is best studied now. Each has two sister chromatids held at the centromere, with disc-shaped kinetochores where spindle fibres attach.
Chromosomes align at the equator; each chromatid's kinetochore is connected to spindle fibres from one pole and its sister's to the opposite pole. The plane of alignment is the metaphase plate.

example.q: At which stage of mitosis would you count chromosomes, and why?
steps: Chromosome condensation is complete at metaphase.

example.answer: Metaphase, when chromosomes are most condensed and clearly visible.

learn.hook: Tender coconut water is liquid endosperm with many free nuclei and no cell walls between them. The nuclei divided, but the cytoplasm never did.
points: Anaphase: each chromosome at the metaphase plate splits simultaneously; centromeres split and the two daughter chromatids (now chromosomes) move to opposite poles, centromere leading and arms trailing.
Telophase: chromosomes at the poles decondense and lose their individuality; a nuclear envelope forms around each cluster, giving two daughter nuclei; the nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform.
Cytokinesis in animal cells: a furrow appears in the plasma membrane, deepens and joins at the centre, dividing the cytoplasm.

Cytokinesis in plant cells: wall formation starts at the centre and grows outward to meet the lateral walls. It begins with a cell plate, which becomes the middle lamella between the walls of the two cells. Organelles such as mitochondria and plastids are distributed to the daughters.
If karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, a multinucleate condition called a syncytium forms, e.g. the liquid endosperm of coconut.

example.q: Why do plant cells form a cell plate instead of a furrow during cytokinesis?
steps: Plant cells are enclosed by a relatively inextensible cell wall.
A furrow cannot pinch a rigid wall inwards.
So a new wall is built from the centre outwards, starting as a cell plate.
example.answer: Their rigid cell wall prevents furrowing, so a cell plate forms from the centre.

learn.reallife: Kerala's tender coconuts sold by the roadside contain liquid endosperm, a natural example of a syncytium.

learn.hook: When you scrape your knee playing cricket, new skin cells form by mitosis to heal it. Mitosis is your built-in repair service.

topics.title: Meiosis and the early stages of prophase I

learn.hook: Why are you not an exact copy of your elder sibling? Part of the answer is a gene swap that happens in pachytene.
points: Meiosis is a reductional division that halves the chromosome number to form haploid cells. It produces the haploid phase in sexually reproducing organisms; fertilisation restores the diploid phase. It occurs during gametogenesis in plants and animals.

Key features: two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division (meiosis I and II) but only one cycle of DNA replication; pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between non-sister chromatids; four haploid cells at the end of meiosis II.
Prophase I is longer and more complex than mitotic prophase and has five sub-stages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.

Leptotene: chromosomes become gradually visible and keep compacting. Zygotene: homologous chromosomes start pairing (synapsis), with formation of a synaptonemal complex; a pair of synapsed homologues is a bivalent or tetrad.

Pachytene (longer than the first two stages): the four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct as tetrads. Recombination nodules appear, where crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. Crossing over is enzyme-mediated (recombinase) and leads to recombination.

example.q: A human primary spermatocyte has 46 chromosomes. How many bivalents form in zygotene?
steps: Each bivalent is a pair of homologous chromosomes.
46 ÷ 2 = 23 bivalents.

learn.reallife: Recombination during pachytene is one reason children of the same parents look different; plant breeders at ICAR rely on it to combine useful traits in new crop varieties.

teach.nudge: Good! In which stage do homologues pair, and when does crossing over happen?

revise.summary: Meiosis halves the chromosome number by two divisions after one DNA replication, giving four haploid cells. Prophase I has five sub-stages: leptotene, zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalents), pachytene (crossing over by recombinase), diplotene and diakinesis.

Crossing over: where, between what, which enzyme

Crossing over: non-sister chromatids of homologues; recombinase
traps: Don't put crossing over in zygotene; it is in pachytene
Don't say crossing over is between sister chromatids

learn.hook: In human females, oocytes pause in diplotene before birth and may stay paused for over a decade until puberty. Patience at the cellular level!
points: Diplotene: the synaptonemal complex dissolves and recombined homologues tend to separate except at crossover sites, which appear as X-shaped chiasmata. In oocytes of some vertebrates, diplotene can last for months or years (this arrested stage is often called dictyotene).

Diakinesis: terminalisation of chiasmata; chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle assembles. By the end, the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down. It is the transition to metaphase.
Metaphase I: bivalents align on the equatorial plate; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the pair of homologous chromosomes.
Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate, while sister chromatids remain together at their centromeres.

Telophase I: the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear, cytokinesis follows, giving a dyad of cells. Interkinesis, the stage between the two meiotic divisions, is generally short and has no DNA replication.

example.q: A cell with 2n = 8 completes meiosis I. How many chromosomes, and how many chromatids per chromosome, does each daughter cell have?
steps: Anaphase I separates homologues, so each cell gets one of each pair: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chromosomes.
Sister chromatids are still joined, so each chromosome has 2 chromatids.

learn.reallife: In human females, oocytes arrested in diplotene before birth resume meiosis only at puberty, a fact gynaecologists use to explain the age-related risk of chromosomal errors.

topics.title: Meiosis II and the significance of meiosis

learn.hook: If gametes were not haploid, chromosome number would double every generation. Meiosis keeps the count steady, generation after generation.
points: Meiosis II starts right after cytokinesis of meiosis I, usually before chromosomes have fully elongated, and resembles normal mitosis. Prophase II: nuclear membrane disappears by its end and chromosomes compact again.

Metaphase II: chromosomes align at the equator; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of sister chromatids. Anaphase II: the centromere of each chromosome splits and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
Telophase II: the two groups of chromosomes are enclosed by nuclear envelopes; cytokinesis follows, giving a tetrad of four haploid daughter cells.
Meiosis I is reductional (homologues separate, halving chromosome number); meiosis II is equational (sister chromatids separate, number stays the same as at the start of meiosis II).

Significance: meiosis conserves the chromosome number of each species across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, although it halves the number in gametes. It increases genetic variability (crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes), which is very important for evolution.

example.q: Why is meiosis II called equational even though it is part of meiosis?
steps: At the start of meiosis II each cell is already haploid (n), each chromosome with two chromatids.
In anaphase II, sister chromatids separate.
Each daughter cell still has n chromosomes, the same as the cell entering meiosis II.
example.answer: Because chromosome number does not change during meiosis II; only sister chromatids separate.

learn.reallife: Variation produced by meiosis is the raw material that let farmers and ICAR scientists select drought-tolerant and disease-resistant crop varieties.

topics.title: Mitosis versus meiosis: comparing and identifying

learn.hook: Exam favourite: 'Identify the stage from the diagram.' Learn the clues once and you'll never confuse anaphase I with anaphase II again.
points: Mitosis: one division, two diploid daughter cells, identical to parent; no pairing or crossing over; occurs in somatic cells for growth and repair.
Meiosis: two divisions, four haploid cells, genetically different; synapsis and crossing over in prophase I; occurs in gamete-forming cells.
Metaphase of mitosis and metaphase II: single chromosomes (two chromatids each) at the equator. Metaphase I: bivalents (paired homologues) at the equator.
Anaphase of mitosis and anaphase II: centromeres split, sister chromatids move apart. Anaphase I: centromeres do not split; homologous chromosomes move apart.
DNA tracking for a 2n cell: G1 2C → after S 4C → after mitosis 2C each; in meiosis, 4C → after meiosis I 2C (n chromosomes) → after meiosis II 1C (n chromosomes).

steps: Chromosomes moving to poles means anaphase.
